title: Buying bread at a bakery in Paris
setting: It's late morning in Montmartre, Paris. The smell of fresh bread leads you into a small boulangerie. A short queue waits at the counter, where the baker is wrapping baguettes in paper.
objectives: Greet shopkeepers the way the French expect
Understand "Et avec ceci ?" and finish your order
Say goodbye the friendly French way
varietyNote: This is everyday French as spoken in Paris and most of France. French varies across France, Belgium, Switzerland, Africa and Canada — in Québec, for example, you'll hear different expressions in shops (see the Montréal adventure).

phrases.translation: Hello! (to a woman — "monsieur" to a man)
phrases.example: Bonjour, monsieur ! Une baguette, s'il vous plaît.
phrases.note: Always say "bonjour" when you walk into a shop. In France, skipping it comes across as rude.

phrases.text: Je voudrais une baguette, s'il vous plaît.
phrases.example: Je voudrais deux croissants, s'il vous plaît.

alsoHeard.where: Short and perfectly polite — once you've said bonjour

phrases.example: Une tradition bien cuite, s'il vous plaît.
phrases.note: Made to a traditional recipe with no additives — crustier and chewier than a classic baguette. Many Parisians ask for theirs "bien cuite" (well baked) or "pas trop cuite" (not too baked).

phrases.example: —Et avec ceci ? —Un pain au chocolat, s'il vous plaît.

phrases.note: In the evening, you'll hear "Bonne soirée !" instead.

cultureNotes: "Bonjour" is essential. Walking into a shop and asking for something without greeting first is one of the most common mistakes visitors make in France.
Adding "madame" or "monsieur" after bonjour sounds warm and polite with shopkeepers.
Bakeries get busy around lunchtime and before dinner, when people pick up fresh bread for the meal.
Small purchases by contactless card are common, but cash is fine too.

steps.text: It's your turn. The baker looks up at you and waits.

steps.prompt: What's the first thing you should do?

options.text: Say "Bonjour, madame !" before asking for anything.
options.why: Exactly. Greeting first is expected in every French shop.

options.text: Point at the bread and say "Baguette."
options.why: You'd get your bread, but skipping the greeting comes across as rude in France.

options.text: Wait silently until she asks what you want.
options.why: In France the customer is expected to greet first — waiting silently can seem cold.

steps.speaker: Baker
steps.text: Bonjour ! Qu'est-ce que je vous sers ?
steps.translation: Hello! What can I get you?

steps.prompt: How do you ask for a baguette?

options.text: Je voudrais une baguette, s'il vous plaît.
options.why: Polite and natural — "je voudrais" (I would like) is the classic way to order.
"Je veux" (I want) sounds blunt in a shop, especially without "s'il vous plaît".
"Give me" sounds demanding, and it's missing "une" (a).

steps.speaker: Baker
steps.translation: A traditional one or a classic one?

options.text: Which kind of baguette you want — traditional or classic
options.why: Right. A "tradition" is made to a traditional recipe and is crustier; a "classique" is the standard baguette.

options.text: Whether you want it wrapped the traditional way
options.why: It's about the bread itself, not the wrapping.
She's asking about the type of baguette, not about you.

steps.prompt: That's all you need. What do you say?

options.why: Polite and natural: "That'll be all, thanks."
This means "It's over / finished" — it sounds like you're ending something, not your order.
"Nothing" on its own is understood but sounds abrupt. Add "merci", or say "ce sera tout".

steps.speaker: Baker
steps.text: Ça fait un euro trente. Merci, bonne journée !
steps.translation: That's €1.30. Thank you, have a good day!

steps.prompt: You pay and take your baguette. How do you say goodbye?

options.why: Warm and polite — exactly what a French customer would say.
"Salut" is for friends. With a shopkeeper it's too informal.
"Bon appétit" is said before someone eats a meal — a bit odd to the baker.
